newsitem.title: taiwan: Taiwan tightens rules on investing in rival China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan tightens rules on investing in rival China.

text.p: Taiwan on Wednesday announced new restrictions on investments in China, including a US$50 million limit on individual projects, but vowed to drop the rules if Beijing renounced the right to retake the island by force.

"At a time when cross-strait (Taiwan-China) relations are so tense, we do not wish to have overly large investments or public construction investments" in the Chinese mainland, economics minister Wang Chih-kang told a news conference.
"But if the Chinese communists announce they are giving up the right to use military force to solve cross-strait problems, I myself believe the restrictions should be dropped," he said.

Communist China regards Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a rebel-held province that must be brought under mainland rule, preferably through peaceful means but by force if the island moves toward independence rather than unification.
Under the rules, Taiwan firms are forbidden from July 1 from investing in Chinese infrastructure projects such as water works, railways, harbours, airports, roads and power plants.
The ministry set a US$50 million ceiling on single-project investments, although it said exceptions could be granted for larger projects that promote "sound interaction" or benefit Taiwan's economy.

The new restrictions throw up major obstacles to Formosa Plastics Group's planned US$3 billion mainland power station, at the core of public debate over Taiwan's political vulnerability in its main rival's market.
Detailed new China investment limits appeared to target the widespread practice of routing investments clandestinely through overseas holding companies, subsidiaries and proxies.

Since a late-1980s political thaw made mainland investments possible, the ministry has reserved a right to approve China projects, ruling that investments by any firm listed in Taiwan's share markets not exceed 40 percent of its paid-in capital.
Until now the ministry had not put a formal ceiling on the size of individual projects.
Taiwan still forbids direct investment and trade with China, a ban dating back to the civil war that split them in 1949.

To date, 30,000 Taiwan firms have legally poured over US$30 billion into China, routing investments through third countries. As a result, Taiwan is now one of China's top overseas investors and China one of Taiwan's most important markets.
Increased political tensions since 1995 have prompted Taiwan to call for more caution in mainland investing, warning against becoming over-dependent on its adversary's economy.
Some big Taiwan firms have called off China projects, though Formosa has given conflicting signals about its intentions.
From July 1, total permitted investments by any listed firm would vary according its size.

Listed firms with net asset value or paid-in capital under T$5 billion (US$179 million) will be allowed to make total investments not exceeding 40 percent of their net asset value or paid-in capital, whichever is higher, the ministry said.
The cap drops to 30 percent for firms between T$5 billion and T$10 billion (US$358 million) and to 20 percent for those whose net asset value or paid-in capital exceeds T$10 billion.

Any unlisted firm with paid-in capital under T$60 million (US$2.2 million) can invest up to T$60 million, while any above T$60 million can invest up to T$60 million or 40 percent of its paid-in capital or net asset value, whichever is higher, the ministry said.
Any listed firm's shareholder acting as an individual can invest a total of no more than T$60 million, the ministry said.
